newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Breakdown of Yugoslav January-May trade.
newsitem.headline: Breakdown of Yugoslav January-May trade.

text.p: Yugoslav trade in the January-May period was near target, with exports up 39 percent and imports 25 percent against the same period last year, the Federal Statistics Office said in its latest report.
The government targeted 40 percent growth in exports and 20 percent in imports for 1997.
Cumulative January-May exports were worth $862 million compared to $620 million the previous year.
Imports in the five-month period stood at $1.709 million compared to $1.362 million in January-May 1996.
Most exports, or $449 million, went to countries in transition, while exports to developed countries were worth $377 million.
Of total exports, $581 million worth were raw materials and semi-finished goods, $239 million consumer goods and $42 investment products.
Most imports, or $842 million, came from developed countries, followed by transition economies from which $663 million worth of goods were imported, and developing countries with $204 million.
In the structure of imports, raw materials and semi-finished goods accounted for $1.179 billion, consumer goods $327 billion and investment products $203 billion.
The highest value of exports was to Italy ($95 million), followed by Germany ($76 million), the Russian Federation ($66 million) and France ($19 million).
Most imports ($233 million) came from Germany, followed by the Russian Federation ($202 million), Italy ($151 million) and France ($42 million).
The Bosnian Serb Republic also accounted for a substantial part of trade with exports worth $183 million and imports $84 million in the five-month period.

Top on the list of exports are ferrous metals ($119.5 million), iron and steel ($88.3 million), fruit and vegetables ($42.4 million), tobacco and tobacco products ($41 million), plastic materials in primary form ($36.4 million) and textiles ($27.7 million).

Imports were dominated by crude oil and oil derivatives ($228.8 million), yarns, fabrics and textile products ($111.5 million), mineral ores and residue ($80.7 million), fruit and vegetables ($73 million), the report said. -- Amra Kevic, Belgrade newsroom +381 11 222 4305
